prompt: What is the first question to ask of a request for a forecast?

choices.text: Which model to use
choices.why: The model depends on the answer to the real first question.

choices.text: What will be decided with it, and when
choices.why: Right. The decision sets the horizon and the grain.

choices.text: How many years of history there are, since more years always make a better forecast
choices.why: History matters, but it does not tell you how far ahead to look.

choices.text: Whether it must be daily
choices.why: The grain follows from the decision, not the other way round.

prompt: Match each of Panela's decisions to the horizon it needs.
The sales director asks the analyst to raise next quarter's forecast by 10 per cent, because that is the team's goal. What is wrong?

choices.text: A target is being written into the forecast column
choices.why: Right. Keep them in separate columns: the kitchen orders from the forecast.

choices.text: Nothing, if the team is confident
choices.why: Confidence is a target. A forecast says what will probably happen.

choices.text: 10 per cent is too large a revision for one quarter
choices.why: The size is not the problem; the reason is.

choices.text: Quarterly forecasts should be made monthly instead
choices.why: The grain is not the issue here.

prompt: Panela needs a monthly figure. Which is usually noisier: thirty daily forecasts added up, or one forecast made on monthly data?

choices.text: The monthly one, because it has twelve times fewer observations to learn from each year
choices.why: Fewer points, but each one is far less noisy, and the decision is monthly.

choices.text: They are always identical, since a month is just the sum of its days
choices.why: The data adds up; the forecast errors do not cancel the same way.

choices.text: It depends only on the model chosen, never on the grain of the data
choices.why: The grain is exactly what changes how errors add up.

choices.text: The summed daily ones
choices.why: Right. Each day's error adds into the month.

prompt: Where should the coverage of a prediction interval be checked?

choices.text: On the weeks the model was fitted on, because there are more of them
choices.why: The model has already seen those, so they flatter it.

choices.text: Nowhere: the software computes the coverage correctly by construction
choices.why: The lesson's back-test found 62 per cent for a nominal 80.

choices.text: On weeks it never saw
choices.why: Right. The same rule as for the forecast itself.

choices.text: On the next year, once it has happened in full
choices.why: That is a fine check, and too late for the decision the interval is for.

prompt: In the lesson's run, what happened to the revisions as the target week approached?

choices.text: They grew larger each time, as more data made the model less certain
choices.why: More data makes it surer, and the revisions shrank.

choices.text: They settled
choices.why: Right. The last vintage was within nine orders of the actual week.

choices.text: Every one of them was exactly zero, because the model had already converged
choices.why: They moved by a few dozen orders, and once by about 200.

choices.text: They alternated up and down
choices.why: One jump and its reversal had a cause; the rest drifted gently.

prompt: Which two reasons make the same model worse a year ahead than a week ahead?

choices.text: Compounded trend error, and more time for events
choices.why: Right. Both add up as the horizon grows.

choices.text: The model forgets its parameters after a few months
choices.why: The parameters are the same at every horizon.

choices.text: Seasons are less regular far ahead
choices.why: The season is the same one projected; it is the world that may change.

choices.text: statsmodels limits the accuracy of long forecasts
choices.why: There is no such limit.

prompt: For the straight trend, what was the mean error, in per cent, 40 to 52 weeks ahead? Answer with the number only.
What does a damped trend assume that a straight one does not?

choices.text: That the series will fall, because every trend eventually turns around and goes down
choices.why: Damping slows growth; it does not reverse it.

choices.text: That there is no season
choices.why: The damped model in the lesson keeps the multiplicative season.

choices.text: That prices will rise
choices.why: No model in the lesson knew about the price rise.

choices.text: That growth slowly flattens
choices.why: Right. Which is rarely wrong for a business a year out.

prompt: The forecast made at the end of 2024 was off by over 20 per cent in the last quarter of 2025. What does that say about the model?

choices.text: It was badly fitted and should be replaced
choices.why: For six months it was within about 5 per cent. The world changed, not the fit.

choices.text: ARIMA would have caught it
choices.why: No model trained on 2023 and 2024 contains the September price rise.

choices.text: Little: the price rise was not in its past
choices.why: Right. Long horizons contain events the past did not.

choices.text: Holt-Winters cannot forecast more than 26 weeks
choices.why: It forecast all 52, and the first 26 were good.

prompt: What is the difference between a confidence interval and a prediction interval?

choices.text: They are two names for one thing
choices.why: statsmodels' method name blurs them, but they answer different questions.

choices.text: A prediction interval keeps one value's own noise
choices.why: Right. A confidence interval is about a fixed quantity and shrinks with data.

choices.text: A confidence interval is always wider
choices.why: It is usually narrower, since it leaves out the noise of a single value.

choices.text: A prediction interval is only for ARIMA
choices.why: Every forecasting method can have one.

prompt: 16 of 26 actual weeks fell inside an 80% interval. What share is that, in per cent, to the nearest whole number?
Why are the intervals software prints usually too narrow?

choices.text: They cover the noise the model expects, and leave out the model being wrong and the parameters being uncertain
choices.why: Right. And the future being unlike the past.

choices.text: They are computed at 50% by default
choices.why: The lesson asked for 80% and 95% explicitly.

choices.text: Rounding
choices.why: Rounding moves an edge by less than one order.

choices.text: Weekly data is too noisy to fit
choices.why: More noise makes intervals wider, not narrower.

prompt: A back-test shows your 80% interval covering 60% of weeks. What is the honest thing to do before showing it?

choices.text: Show it as it is, since the software computed it
choices.why: The software's assumptions were just shown to be wrong on this series.

choices.text: Call it a 60% interval
choices.why: That is at least true, but the decision asked for 80%.

choices.text: Drop intervals and show only the forecast
choices.why: That hides the uncertainty instead of fixing its size.

choices.text: Widen it until it covers 80%, and say so
choices.why: Right. Checked and corrected, openly.

prompt: A manager complains that the June forecast keeps changing every month. What is the best reply?

choices.text: We will freeze it from now on
choices.why: Freezing throws away what the new weeks say.

choices.text: The method is unreliable and will be replaced
choices.why: Revisions of a few dozen orders are what a working method does.

choices.text: Each month adds data, and it uses it
choices.why: Right. Revision is the forecast working.

choices.text: Only the first forecast counts
choices.why: The latest one uses the most information.

prompt: The February vintage of the June forecast jumped by about 200 orders, and the March vintage took it back. Why?

choices.text: Random noise in the fitting
choices.why: The jump has a name, which is the point of the section.

choices.text: A February week came in high without Carnival, and Carnival then arrived in March
choices.why: Right. The level rose on the missing Carnival and fell back when it came.

choices.text: The model changed from straight to damped
choices.why: Every vintage used the same model.

choices.text: The price rise
choices.why: That came in September, after the target week.

prompt: What is lost when each new forecast overwrites the old one? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Knowing what the forecast said when the budget was set
choices.why: Right: accountability.

choices.text: Measuring error at each horizon
choices.why: Right: that needs the forecast as made at that horizon.

choices.text: Seeing whether a method is always optimistic months out
choices.why: Right: learning.

choices.text: The latest forecast itself
choices.why: Overwriting keeps the latest and loses the rest.

prompt: A forecast stored with the date it was made is called a ___.
Order the forecast quarters of 2025 from smallest to largest mean error, for the straight trend.
trap: The first quarter holds New Year and a misplaced Carnival, which is why it is not the most accurate.

prompt: An 80% interval runs from 8,528 to 9,341 orders. How wide is it, in orders?
A report shows next month's and next December's forecasts side by side, in the same font. What should change?

choices.text: Show each with its own interval
choices.why: Right. The horizon belongs in the number.

choices.text: Nothing, if both come from the same model
choices.why: The same model is much less sure far ahead.

choices.text: December's should be removed
choices.why: Finance needs it; it needs its uncertainty with it.

choices.text: Both should be rounded to thousands
choices.why: Rounding hides the problem without describing it.
